## TL;DR


-


**Multi-sig beats single-seed custody.** Ledger’s supply chain hack illustrates why independent keys would have left an attacker in the dark.


-


**Tokenized Treasuries as repo collateral.** BNY and Citadel demonstrate that the capital efficiency is real, but interoperability is still an open question.


-


**Fink’s world and what it means for bitcoin.** Capital scarcity and rising real yields raise the hurdle for bitcoin, but record debt strengthens the longer-term case for scarce assets outside government control.


## Fool Me Twice: Ledger’s Supply Chain Hack and the Case for Multi-sig


Self-custody holders are reeling from a second major hardware wallet loss in ten weeks, this time from tampered Ledger devices that onchain analysis says cost between $86 million and $102 million. The July failure at Coldcard came from weak entropy in seed generation, a flaw in the math. The Ledger losses came from a supply chain attack, in which a covert implant inside devices sold by a single reseller captured recovery phrases as owners set them up. The failures differ, but the exposure is the same. In both cases one seed on one device was all an attacker needed. Both of these types of attacks could have been thwarted by having multi-sig as a standard to prevent single points of failure.


## Tampered Ledger Devices Sold Through One Reseller Drained an Estimated $100 Million


On October 9th, Ledger said it was investigating reports of drained wallets tied to devices sold by CryptoBilis, a reseller covering Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, and asked the company to halt sales and shipments. The following day, Ledger verified an unauthorized hardware implant inside at least one affected device. By October 11th, it said every confirmed case traced back to CryptoBilis purchases while its own systems and direct sales were unaffected. On October 13th, the company explained the infiltration mechanism. A covert component inserted inside the device enclosure used a microcontroller to decode the recovery phrase as it appeared on the screen during setup, then transmitted the words over the cellphone network to the attacker. Ledger describes the episode as a physical supply chain attack and says it has no indication that its software or internal systems were compromised.


Loss estimates differ by source, with blockchain data provider[Bitquery](https://bitquery.io/investigations/ledger-cryptobilis-hack) putting the total at $102 million across 324 wallets on six networks, including roughly $79.3 million on TRON, $16.8 million in bitcoin and $3.7 million on Ethereum, while earlier analyst estimates were closer to $86 million. Although the estimates differ, the onchain record points to planning of the attack. Bitquery shows the theft addresses were funded on September 25th and ran test transactions through October 7th, so the operation appears to have been prepared well before the first public report.


CryptoBilis is a Kuala Lumpur-based reseller whose former founders say they handed operational control to new management in March 2026, and it has since suspended sales of all hardware wallets. Whether that change of hands has anything to do with the tampering is unknown. Ledger has not said where the devices were altered, whether in transit, at the reseller or earlier in the chain, and security researchers have reported suspicious modifications in wallets bought elsewhere that Ledger has not confirmed. A hardware wallet is sold as the product that allows for self-custody and cold storage, which makes its failure a heartbreaking event for the community.


## Coldcard Suffered from Broken Entropy, Ledger Suffered from Broken Distribution


July’s Coldcard incident was a technical failure. A build error left seeds generated between March 2021 and July 2026 with weak entropy, so attackers rebuilt private keys offline without touching a device. That flaw sat in firmware code that an audit could in principle have found, and owners who added their own dice rolls were spared. Ledger’s owners had no comparable lever, because the compromise sat in the hardware before the box was opened, and Ledger itself says its Genuine Check feature cannot detect an added implant. Neither problem can be repaired with an update, since patched Coldcard firmware does not fix a seed already generated and Ledger’s affected buyers are told to abandon the device. What the two share is the single-signature model, in which one seed on one device is the whole of the security, and a holder cannot rule out a flawed generator or a compromised supply chain from the outside.


## Multi-sig Turns One Compromised Device into Just One Compromised Key


A multi-sig wallet requires signatures from several keys before funds can move, and the keys can live on devices from different vendors bought through different channels. The Ledger implant harvested one seed per device, so an attacker who tampered with a single device in a 2-of-3 structure would hold only one key of the three needed. Even if a single Ledger device was affected, remaining signatures could have stayed out of reach.


Spending from a 2-of-3 also requires the wallet’s configuration, which lists all three cosigner public keys. An attacker holding two seeds can derive two of those keys but still needs the third. Since public keys are not secret and are often stored alongside backups or exposed by prior transactions, we treat this as friction rather than a safeguard.


The Coldcard episode offers another look. Unchained reported that 2-of-3 users were shielded from immediate risk when the Coldcard flaw surfaced, because a single weak key could not meet the threshold. A single-signature wallet gets no such protection, and the Coldcard sweeps ran in a window short enough that owners with one key had little chance to react. A multi-sig holder with one bad key has time to retire the signer and rotate to a clean one.


Other controls help at the margin. Ledger says every confirmed drain traces to CryptoBilis and no reports involve devices bought directly from the company, so buying from the manufacturer would have avoided the exposure entirely. That advice depends on the buyer knowing which channels to trust before anything has gone wrong, and on every device in a treasury having come through them. Multi-sig asks less of the holder, since the structure protects the funds even when the holder cannot say which device is the bad one.


Multi-sig has limits. If all signers use devices from one vendor or a compromised reseller, an attacker may gain enough keys to meet the signing threshold. It also cannot protect signers who are tricked into approving a malicious transaction. In the 2024 WazirX theft, attackers changed the wallet’s smart contract and drained $234.9 million without using the signers’ keys. The best defense is diversity of vendor, purchasing channel, geography and entropy source, paired with an independent check on what each signer is authorizing, or a custody provider that employs multi-sig, like BitGo.


## Test Case Highlights the Benefits of Tokenized Securities


On October 13th, BNY[announced](https://www.bny.com/corporate/global/en/about-us/newsroom/press-release/bny-completes-tokenized-us-treasury-triparty-repo-workflow-with-citadel-securities.html) that it had completed a **triparty repo** workflow with Citadel Securities using a tokenized representation of a U.S. Treasury, which BNY called the first use of tokenized assets on a major triparty repo platform. Citadel purchased a 2-year Treasury note through BNY on Tradeweb. After execution, a tokenized representation of the security was recorded on BNY’s private digital ledger and settled within minutes, rather than on the standard T+1 cycle. Citadel then pledged the token as collateral in an overnight triparty repo, with BNY providing cash in return. A single note therefore went from trade to settlement to short-term financing.


### Collateral Management Is the Real Unlock


BNY frames the trade as tokenized assets moving beyond issuance and settlement into core collateral and financing workflows, which is a huge capital efficiency gain for financial services companies. The use case is worth taking seriously because repo is where much of the Treasury market’s plumbing resides. If a security can settle in minutes and be pledged immediately, the gap between owning an asset and being able to fund it narrows, and that gap has a cost for any balance sheet that carries it.


The structural argument is that markets are becoming more continuous and efficient, enabled by tokenized securities. BNY also plans to extend operating hours on its Fed-eligible securities and U.S. triparty platforms, with a view to reaching European and Asian hours next year, and it describes tokenization and extended hours as evolving together to enable more continuous market activity.


For the industry, the question is less whether Treasuries get tokenized and more how capital efficiency benefits market participants.


### BNY’s Ledger Is Private, and That Is Both the Point and the Limit


The token in this trade lived on BNY’s private digital ledger, which is very different from the open, permissionless platforms most are accustomed to in the digital assets realm. A closed loop run by one bank is a faster version of the existing system, not an open one, and nothing in the announcement explains how the tokenized representation would move to other ledgers. The bank also says it plans to introduce additional digital cash and tokenized deposit capabilities for onchain settlement and financing. The open question is interoperability, and it will determine whether this becomes a feature of one bank’s platform or a layer of the broader market.


### Tokenized Securities Are a Big Deal


Tokenized securities are one of the more consequential trends in institutional markets, and the benefits are getting hard to dismiss. BitGo was not part of BNY’s transaction, but it is involved in this market from the custody and settlement side, around assets that sit outside bank-run ledgers.


BitGo’s[relationship with DTCC](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/inside-the-infrastructure-powering-dtccs-tokenized-securities-milestone/) is the clearest example. In July, DTCC ran a limited production event for its Tokenization Service, an end-to-end workflow for DTC-tokenized U.S. Treasuries and equities. BitGo Bank & Trust, which BitGo describes as the only OCC-regulated, full-service qualified custodian integrated with the service, custodied the tokenized securities and supported settlement for repo and reverse repo transactions. BNY’s trade this week is a closely related use case, but in BitGo’s case the assets came from DTCC rather than a bank ledger.


While implementations may differ, we think the more important point is that existing market infrastructure is increasingly building tokenization into its own plumbing. BNY did it on a private ledger and DTCC is doing it through its Tokenization Service. The benefit that stands out most to us is capital efficiency. When a Treasury settles in minutes and can then be pledged as collateral, less capital sits idle waiting on a settlement cycle. The open question is whether collateral can move between these ledgers, and that will determine how much of the efficiency gain is realized.


## Fink Speaks, Market Listens: Implications for Bitcoin and Digital Assets


This week, BlackRock reported third quarter earnings, and the call gave investors a rare look at CEO Larry Fink’s read on markets and the macro backdrop. His view of the global economy is worth unpacking, particularly for what it means for bitcoin and other digital assets. We reviewed the call and distilled his most important observations below, along with how each could affect bitcoin.


### Capital Scarcity Is About Competition


Fink’s point is about competition more than a drought. Governments need financing for deficits, companies need to fund a generational AI buildout, and individuals need better ways to retire. He put the U.S. need for power, grid, and core and shell construction at $7 trillion to $9 trillion, and a 1 gigawatt data center at roughly $50 billion. When claims on capital outgrow supply, the price of capital rises, and that price is the hurdle every asset has to clear.


Bitcoin funds nothing and throws off no cash flow, so in a market rationing capital toward projects with identifiable returns, it has to earn its place on diversification and scarcity alone. Digital asset ETPs took in $8 billion this quarter, under 4% of BlackRock’s $205 billion of net inflows. We see this as a headwind at the margin, not a thesis-breaker. Scarcity of capital and scarcity of bitcoin are different things, and only one of them shows up in real yields.


### Fiscal Backdrop Creates Argument for Bitcoin


Record borrowing and a contest for capital are the conditions behind the long-running case for a scarce asset outside government control. Fink never made that case, so we are borrowing his backdrop and not his conclusion. His best case, growth strong enough to shrink debt-to-GDP, would also take some of the urgency out of it.


He sees structurally higher rates as the result, which could weigh on bitcoin in the near term. But the long-running case for scarce assets outside government control rests on these same deficits, and higher rates do not make it go away.


### Real Yields Near 3% Compete Directly with Bitcoin


Bitcoin pays no direct yield, so every rise in real rates raises the cost of holding it. The point was hammered home by the fact that fixed income took in $78 billion of net inflows in the quarter, against $8 billion for digital asset ETPs. The products serve different purposes, so this does not show bitcoin losing share, but it does show where the marginal dollar went.


### Risk-on/Risk-off Regime Shift


BlackRock’s CFO, Martin Small, said “I don't believe we can evaluate the investment environment as risk-on or risk-off any longer.” What matters now is capital allocation, financing advantages, and a redesign of diversification. Bitcoin has often been sorted into the risk-on bucket, so dropping that switch means it gets judged on what it adds next to everything else. The diversifiers he highlighted were private markets and liquid alternatives, though, not crypto.


### Growth Escape Velocity as the Savior


Fink’s way out of our financial condition is growth,[aligned](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/bessent-we-can-grow-our-way-out-of-debt-with-3-gdp-growth-230032528.html) with the Treasury head Scott Bessent’s view. If financing the AI buildout lifts the economy to 3% or better, debt to GDP falls and the debt matters less.


For bitcoin, this cuts several ways. Stronger growth helps risk appetite. It also reduces the urgency of the debasement argument. And faster growth tends to come with higher real rates, at least at first, so the escape valve could ease the fiscal worry while leaving the yield headwind in place. The best case for the economy is not automatically the best case for bitcoin. The version that helps most is one where growth is firm and real yields stop rising.


### Conclusion


Fink never mentioned bitcoin, but the world he described is the one bitcoin has to compete in. A market short on capital, carrying record debt and facing higher rates for longer, raises the bar for any asset that pays nothing. The same conditions strengthen the long-running case for scarce assets outside government control. We think near-term price will follow the first force and the longer-term thesis will follow the second. For investors, the practical question is whether bitcoin earns its place in a portfolio when capital carries a real return near 3%.
